claims.text: An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a business opportunity and takes the risk of starting and running a business, organising the workers, premises, equipment and money it needs, in the hope of earning profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Successful entrepreneurs tend to share characteristics such as hard work, creativity, a willingness to take calculated risks, optimism, self-confidence and the ability to communicate well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: These characteristics matter because a new business is uncertain: the founder who works hard, checks the market before committing money and keeps trying after setbacks is more likely to survive the early years than one who does not.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business plan is a written document setting out a business idea, the people behind it, its objectives, its market, its operations and its financial forecasts, usually written before the business starts trading.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business plan usually includes a description of the product or service, the entrepreneur and team, the aims of the business, a marketing plan, an operations plan and financial forecasts, and strong plans also name the competition and foreseeable risks.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business plan assists the entrepreneur in two main ways: writing it forces the idea to be researched and tested on paper before money is committed, and a finished plan is evidence that a lender is more likely to accept, because it shows the thinking behind the numbers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Governments commonly support start-ups through grants tied to a purpose, training schemes in costing, marketing and record-keeping, cheap premises in small-business centres, and advisory services.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Governments support start-ups because new businesses create jobs and incomes, produce goods and services, pay tax, and can revive regions where unemployment is high.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Government support lowers the cost and skills barriers a start-up faces without the state taking ownership or control: grants and training places leave decisions and profit with the entrepreneur, unlike state involvement in running a company.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Support has limits that a founder should weigh: grants may be conditional on location or sector, training schemes take time the business also needs, and not every applicant qualifies.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Business size is commonly measured in three ways: the number of people employed, the value of output over a period, and capital employed - the money invested in the business's assets. Profit is not a measure of size; it measures how well the business is doing.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Profit is not a method of measuring business size: profit measures performance, so a vast business can be loss-making and a tiny one profitable.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The three measures can rank the same two businesses differently, because production methods differ: a capital-intensive firm may lead on output value and capital employed while a labour-intensive rival leads on people employed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each measure has weaknesses: employment ignores how a business produces and the mix of part-time and full-time staff; value of output swells with bought-in materials; capital employed depends heavily on the trade.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Because each measure sees only one dimension of size, no single measure reliably settles which business is bigger; used together, the measures give a fairer comparison.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Expansion means increasing the scale of a business's operations - producing more output, serving more customers, opening more outlets or extending the product range - so the business becomes larger than before.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Owners commonly want to expand for higher profit, a larger market share, lower unit costs as fixed costs spread over more output, reduced risk from selling in more markets, and personal status and satisfaction.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Expansion and rising profit are not the same thing: growth is a change in the scale of operations while profit is what remains after every cost, and a growing business may be busier and poorer for years if the extra revenue does not outrun the extra costs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal (organic) growth is expansion achieved with the business's own resources, such as new outlets or an extended product range; external growth is expansion by joining with another business through a merger or a takeover.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal growth tends to be slower but keeps ownership and control unchanged, while external growth delivers size quickly but needs large finance and requires two organisations to be integrated.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A merger is an agreed combination of two businesses into one; a takeover is one business buying control of another.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Problems linked to growth include the need for finance before the growth pays, finding and training new staff, weakened control and communication as layers grow, diseconomies of scale past the size the business can coordinate, thinning personal service, and money tied up in the expansion before the extra revenue arrives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Growth problems can be overcome by phased expansion, training before opening, delegating authority to local managers, shortening reporting lines, standardising systems and restructuring when unit costs creep up as coordination thins.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Diseconomies of scale are the rises in average cost that can hit a business once it grows beyond the size its structure can coordinate: communication slows, motivation falls and duplicated effort spreads, so each unit costs more even though output is larger.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses remain small because the market itself is small, the owner's objectives are modest, personal service is the product, or the trade gains little cost advantage from size - and some remain small unwillingly, for want of growth finance or management skill.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Staying small can be a deliberate success: a business that funds the owner's chosen life, keeps control close and matches its market's size meets the objectives its owner actually set, whereas forced smallness is often close to failure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business fails when it stops trading because it can no longer cover its costs; insolvency, the state of being unable to pay debts as they fall due, is the harder edge of failure.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main causes of business failure are weak management of pricing and records, changes in the business environment such as new competitors, cost rises or shifting demand, and liquidity problems - and the causes compound one another.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Liquidity problems arise when cash does not match the timing of the bills: a business can be profitable on paper and still fail, because profit and cash are not the same thing - profit is earned across a period while cash arrives on particular days.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: New businesses face a greater risk of failure because they start with no customer base, no trading record, untested forecasts and thin reserves, and they often lean on one product, one location and one owner.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Suppliers typically want cash up front from a firm with no trading history while established rivals enjoy time to pay, so a young firm's costs arrive earlier; one bad month can end a venture whose owner staked personal savings.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An established business has spread its risks across products and customers and can show a trading record, which is why the risk of failure falls with each year a business survives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capital employed and working capital measure different things: capital employed is the total money invested in a business's assets and is one measure of its size, while working capital is current assets minus current liabilities - the short-term money available to run the business day to day - and is not a measure of size.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
